key_terms.meaning: Signed number of moles of species i produced per mole of reaction; negative for reactants, positive for products
Reaction-progress variable in mol; nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ for every species
The smallest set of reactions that can produce every observed composition change; count R = N − rank(A), where N = number of species and A = the atomic (element) matrix
Total moles n = n₀ + ξ Σνᵢ, so mole fractions yᵢ = (nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ) / (n₀ + ξΣνᵢ)
Partial molar Gibbs energy of species i, μᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ) at fixed T, P and other n's; units J/mol
At fixed T and P in a closed system, equilibrium is where total G is minimum, i.e. (∂G/∂ξ) = 0, equivalently Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 (Aᵢ = affinity = 0)
Dimensionless measure of a species relative to its standard state; μᵢ = G°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ
The reference state at which aᵢ = 1: pure gas at 1 bar behaving ideally, pure liquid or solid at 1 bar, solute at 1 molal or 1 molar as chosen
ΔG° = ΣνᵢG°ᵢ, the reaction Gibbs energy when every species is in its standard state; depends on T only
K = exp(−ΔG°/RT) = Π aᵢ^νᵢ at equilibrium; a pure number at a given temperature
d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/(RT²); equivalently d(ln K)/d(1/T) = −ΔH°/R
ΔH° = ΣνᵢH°ᵢ; its sign decides whether K rises (endothermic) or falls (exothermic) with temperature
ln K = −ΔG°/(RT) = −ΔH°/(RT) + ΔS°/R, using standard free energies of formation at the temperature of interest
Q = Π aᵢ^νᵢ at the actual (non-equilibrium) composition; Q < K means the forward reaction is feasible, Q > K means the reverse
Fraction of the limiting reactant converted at equilibrium; for A → products with ν_A = −1, X = (n_A0 − n_A)/n_A0
Yield = moles of desired product formed per mole of limiting reactant fed; selectivity = desired product per competing undesired product
For gases K = K_y K_p^(Σν), with K_y = Π yᵢ^νᵢ; raising P shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles when Σν < 0
Adding an inert raises total moles, lowers every yᵢ, and pushes equilibrium toward the side with more gas moles
φᵢ = f̂ᵢ /(yᵢP) with f̂ᵢ = yᵢφᵢP; for ideal gases φᵢ = 1 and K becomes K_p in bars
With R independent reactions, equilibrium needs R equations Σᵢνᵢⱼμᵢ = 0, j = 1…R, plus element balances, solved for ξ₁…ξ_R

takeaways: A reacting mixture needs only stoichiometric coefficients and one extent variable per independent reaction to fix every mole number.
At fixed T and P a closed reacting system stops changing when total Gibbs energy is minimum, which is the same statement as Σνᵢμᵢ = 0.
The standard Gibbs energy change sets K through ΔG° = −RT ln K, and K itself depends only on temperature, never on pressure or initial composition.
Van't Hoff's equation turns tabulated ΔH° data into K at any other temperature; endothermic reactions are favoured by heating, exothermic ones by cooling.
K is a number, not a composition: converting it to conversions needs activities, mole balances and, for gases, the pressure and inert content.
Q versus K decides feasibility at the current composition; equilibrium conversion and yield say how far the feed can actually go.
Raising pressure helps only reactions that reduce the number of gas moles; inert dilution always works against them and is best removed by purge.
Real problems stack nonideality, several phases and several reactions, so each reaction gets its own equilibrium relation over one shared set of mole balances.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to move from the Gibbs-minimisation criterion to the K expression, then apply van't Hoff, pressure and inert effects, and finish with numerical conversion or multireaction balances.

bank.q: Define the extent of reaction and show that a reacting mixture with N species and R independent reactions needs exactly R extent variables. How is R found from the atomic matrix?
outline: Write nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + Σⱼνᵢⱼξⱼ for R reactions.
State that each ξⱼ runs from 0 upward and stops where a reactant hits zero.
Build the element-by-species atomic matrix A and note that element balances conserve atoms for every ξ set.
Independent reactions = N − rank(A); explain that dependent reactions add no new composition change.
Give one worked count, e.g. N species with two elements and rank 2.

bank.q: Derive the equilibrium criterion Σνᵢμᵢ = 0 for a closed system held at fixed temperature and pressure, starting from dG.
outline: Write dG = −S dT + V dP + Σμᵢ dnᵢ.
At fixed T and P the first two terms vanish, leaving dG = Σμᵢ dnᵢ.
Substitute dnᵢ = νᵢ dξ to get dG = (Σνᵢμᵢ) dξ.
At equilibrium G is minimum, so dG/dξ = 0, hence Σνᵢμᵢ = 0; second derivative positive for a stable minimum.
Note the affinity A = −Σνᵢμᵢ drives the reaction and vanishes at equilibrium.
Mention that for open or non-P-T-constrained systems a different potential is minimised (A at fixed T, V).

bank.q: Define standard state and activity, and derive K = Π aᵢ^νᵢ from μᵢ = G°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ.
outline: Define standard state for gas, liquid and solid; aᵢ = 1 there.
Write μᵢ = G°ᵢ + RT ln aᵢ and substitute into Σνᵢμᵢ = 0.
Collect ΣνᵢG°ᵢ = ΔG° and Σνᵢ ln aᵢ = ln Π aᵢ^νᵢ.
Obtain ΔG° = −RT ln K with K = Π aᵢ^νᵢ at equilibrium.
Point out K is dimensionless and depends on T only, not on P or feed.

bank.q: The equilibrium constant of a reaction is K₁ at T₁. Using van't Hoff's equation, obtain K₂ at T₂ for (a) constant ΔH° and (b) ΔH° varying linearly with temperature.
outline: Start from d(ln K)/dT = ΔH°/(RT²).
Case (a): integrate to ln(K₂/K₁) = −(ΔH°/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁).
Substitute numbers with ΔH° in J/mol and T in kelvin; state the sign convention for exothermic reactions.
Case (b): write ΔH°(T) = ΔH°₀ + ΔC°p (T − T₀) and integrate term by term.
Comment that K falls with rising T when ΔH° < 0 and rises when ΔH° > 0.
Warn that the integrated form is exact only for the assumed ΔH° behaviour.

bank.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ with a stoichiometric feed at 700 K and 200 bar, write the equilibrium relation in terms of conversion and calculate the equilibrium conversion for a given K.
outline: Take basis 1 mol N₂ + 3 mol H₂, ξ = X with X the fractional conversion of N₂.
Moles: N₂ = 1 − X, H₂ = 3 − 3X, NH₃ = 2X, total = 4 − 2X.
Mole fractions from the total; note Σν = −2.
Write K = K_y K_p^(−2) = [y_NH₃² /(y_N₂ y_H₂³)] (P/P°)⁻².
Insert yᵢ(X) to get one algebraic equation in X; solve numerically and keep the root in 0 ≤ X < 1.
State the result as a conversion with units of mol N₂ converted per mol fed.

bank.q: Explain and illustrate how total pressure and inert addition change the equilibrium conversion of a gas reaction whose Σν is negative, keeping temperature fixed.
outline: K is fixed at fixed T; only K_y can change with P and inerts.
K = K_y K_p^Σν ⇒ K_y = K (P/P°)^(−Σν).
For Σν < 0, raising P raises K_y and hence conversion.
Adding inerts lowers all yᵢ, lowers K_y, and shifts equilibrium backward for Σν < 0.
Show the yᵢ expressions with the inert mole number in the total.
Industrial note: purge inert gas to protect conversion; high pressure is used in ammonia synthesis for this reason.

bank.q: A liquid-phase reaction A + B ⇌ C is run at 350 K with nonideal solution behaviour. Show how K is converted to a composition relation and how activity coefficients enter.
outline: K = a_C/(a_A a_B) with aᵢ = γᵢxᵢ.
So K = (γ_C/γ_Aγ_B)(x_C/x_A x_B) = K_γ K_x.
Since liquids are incompressible, pressure has almost no effect on K; the standard state is the pure liquid at 1 bar.
K_x = K/K_γ requires γᵢ from a model (Margules, van Laar, NRTL, UNIFAC).
Solve K_x with the mole balance xᵢ = (nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ)/n_total for ξ.
Note dilute solutes need a Henry-based standard state instead.

bank.q: Carbon monoxide is shifted with steam: CO + H₂O ⇌ CO₂ + H₂, with a side reaction CO + 3H₂ ⇌ CH₄ + H₂O. Set up the multireaction equilibrium problem.
outline: Identify two independent reactions; check R = N − rank(A) with species CO, H₂O, CO₂, H₂, CH₄.
Introduce ξ₁ and ξ₂; write every nᵢ and total moles.
Write two equilibrium relations K₁ = Π aᵢ^νᵢ¹ and K₂ = Π aᵢ^νᵢ² at the same T.
Add carbon, hydrogen and oxygen balances; show only two are independent.
Solve the coupled nonlinear equations in ξ₁, ξ₂ numerically; compare with Gibbs minimisation.
Note Σν = 0 for the shift reaction, so pressure leaves that one unaffected.

bank.q: A gas mixture of known composition is held at a given T and P for a reaction with known K. Explain how you would decide whether the forward reaction, the reverse reaction or nothing happens.
outline: Compute the reaction quotient Q = Π aᵢ^νᵢ from the actual composition.
Compare Q with K: Q < K forward feasible, Q > K reverse feasible, Q = K at equilibrium.
Relate the sign of ΔG = RT ln(Q/K) to the direction; negative ΔG means the forward direction is spontaneous.
State that K depends only on T, so temperature decides how far the system can go while Q sets the starting point.
Mention that a large negative ΔG° does not fix the conversion — thermodynamics and kinetics are separate questions.

bank.q: Discuss the choice between K_p, K_y and K_a for gas-phase equilibria, and assess when fugacity coefficients can be ignored.
outline: Define f̂ᵢ = yᵢφᵢP and K = Π (f̂ᵢ/fᵢ°)^νᵢ.
At low pressure φᵢ → 1 so K ≈ K_p = Π (yᵢP/P°)^νᵢ.
Write K = K_y K_φ (P/P°)^Σν to separate composition, nonideality and pressure.
Judging rule: ignore φᵢ near 1 bar; at 100 bar and above use an equation of state or generalised charts.
Example: ammonia synthesis at 200–300 bar has φᵢ far from unity.
Conclusion: K_a is the rigorous constant; K_p and K_y are approximations valid in stated limits.

bank.q: For a heterogeneous reaction such as CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g), derive the equilibrium relation and explain why solids drop out of K.
outline: Write K = a_CO₂ a_CaO / a_CaCO₃ with each pure solid at unit activity.
Activity of a pure solid at 1 bar is 1, so K = a_CO₂ = f̂_CO₂/f° ≈ p_CO₂/P°.
Hence the decomposition pressure is fixed by T alone, giving K = p_CO₂/P° and p_CO₂ = K P°.
Show that adding or removing solid changes nothing at equilibrium as long as both phases persist.
Distinguish cases where a solid is consumed completely, where the activity term no longer applies.
Link to calcination temperature in lime kilns and to the phase rule for reacting systems.

bank.q: Compare the two routes to multireaction equilibrium — solving R equations Σνᵢⱼμᵢ = 0 with element balances, and direct Gibbs energy minimisation — and assess their merits.
outline: Route 1: choose R independent reactions, write R equilibrium constants plus element balances, solve for R extents.
Route 2: minimise G = Σnᵢμᵢ(nᵢ) subject to element balances, using Lagrange multipliers.
Show both use the same μᵢ model and give the same answer.
Advantage of minimisation: no need to guess a reaction set; danger of local minima and numerical stiffness.
Advantage of K-equations: physically transparent, easier to start, but needs known independent reactions.
Mention extent bounds nᵢ ≥ 0 and that nonnegativity constraints matter in practical solvers.

bank.q: Assess how temperature, pressure and inert level together set the equilibrium conversion in an industrial gas reaction with Σν < 0 and ΔH° < 0.
outline: ΔH° < 0 means K falls as T rises, so low T favours conversion but slows kinetics.
Σν < 0 means high P favours conversion through K_y = K(P/P°)^(−Σν).
Inerts dilute the mixture and cut conversion, so a purge stream is needed.
Optimal design therefore compromises with a moderate T, high P and low inert level.
Write the general K = K_y K_φ (P/P°) ^Σν relation and show each lever's role.
Note that reaction kinetics, catalyst life and compression cost set the practical limits.

bank.q: State the phase rule and Duhem's theorem for reacting systems and explain what they allow you to fix when designing an equilibrium calculation.
outline: Degrees of freedom F = C − P + 2 − R for a system with R independent reactions.
Explain why each independent reaction removes one degree of freedom: it adds a relation Σνᵢμᵢ = 0.
Duhem's theorem: fixing two independent intensive properties fixes the entire intensive state of a closed system, reacting or not.
Consequence: composition at equilibrium follows from T and P plus feed and element balances.
Give an example, e.g. a two-phase reacting mixture where T and P fix all phase compositions.

glossary.def: A single variable ξ in mol that measures how far a reaction has run; every mole number follows from nᵢ = nᵢ₀ + νᵢξ.
The fixed molar ratios in which species appear in a balanced chemical equation.
The reactant that runs out first and therefore caps the maximum possible conversion.
The state in which no further net change of composition occurs at fixed temperature and pressure.
The partial molar Gibbs energy of a species, equal to the change in G when one mole is added at fixed T, P and other amounts.
A = −Σνᵢμᵢ in J/mol; positive when the forward reaction is spontaneous, zero at equilibrium.
The numerical method of finding equilibrium composition by minimising total G subject to element balances.
The agreed reference state, at unit activity, against which Gibbs energies and activities are measured.
The dimensionless effective amount of a species relative to its standard state; equals 1 for a pure liquid or solid at 1 bar.
An effective pressure that makes the ideal-gas chemical potential formula work for real gases.
The temperature-dependent number K = Π aᵢ^νᵢ evaluated at equilibrium; related to ΔG° by ΔG° = −RT ln K.
ΔG°f of a compound: the change in Gibbs energy when one mole forms from elements in their standard states.
A reaction with ΔH° > 0; its equilibrium constant rises as temperature rises.
A reaction with ΔH° < 0; its equilibrium constant falls as temperature rises.
Q = Π aᵢ^νᵢ at the actual composition; comparison with K tells the direction of change.
The fraction of the fed limiting reactant that has reacted when equilibrium is reached.
The fraction of reacted feed that ends up as the desired product rather than a by-product.
The equilibrium constant expressed in partial pressures, K_p = Π(pᵢ/p°)^νᵢ, valid for ideal gases.
The equilibrium constant expressed in mole fractions, K_y = Π yᵢ^νᵢ; carries all the composition dependence for gases.
A species present in the mixture that takes no part in the reaction but adds to the total moles.
A minimal set of reactions whose extents can describe every possible composition change of the system.
A reaction involving more than one phase, so each pure condensed phase contributes unit activity.
Fixing any two independent intensive properties of a closed system fixes all its remaining intensive properties.
F = C − P + 2 − R, where C counts components, P counts phases and R counts independent reactions.
